title: Every Time God Was About to Do Something Impossible, He Started Here First
fullText: I want to show you something I found in the Bible that I cannot unsee. Every time God was about to do something impossible, and I mean the biggest miracles in all of scripture, he started in the same place first, not similar places. Not comparable situations, the same place every time without exception. The Red Sea did not part when Israel had options. It parted when they had none. The fire did not fall on Elijah's altar when it was dry. It fell after he soaked it with 12 barrels of water in the middle of a 3-year drought. Lazarus was not raised when he was sick. He was raised 4 days after he was buried, after even his sister said, "Lord, by now he stinkketh." The feeding of 5,000 didn't happen when the disciples had food. It happened after they told Jesus it was impossible. Gideon didn't defeat the Midianites with the 32,000 men he assembled. God made him send them home, all of them, until 300 were left against an army described as thick as locusts. Look at that pattern long enough and something becomes clear. God does not begin with plenty. He begins with nothing. Not almost nothing. Nothing. The moment when every human option is exhausted. The moment when hope has a funeral, that is where God starts. And if your life looks like that right now, if you are staring at a situation where nothing is left, I need you to hear this because what you are calling too late may be exactly what God has been waiting for. Before we go through the stories, I need to establish the principle because without it, everything I'm about to say sounds like motivational noise dressed up in Bible verses. Here it is. God doesn't just tolerate impossible situations, he engineers them. Look at Exodus 14. When Israel left Egypt, God did not lead them by the shortest route to Canaan. Scripture is explicit about this. He deliberately led them south toward the Red Sea away from safety. And then he told Moses to have them camp in a specific location, Phyahroth, between Mdal and the sea. And he told Moses exactly why Pharaoh will think the Israelites are wandering in confusion, hemmed in by the desert. God set the trap. Not Pharaoh. God. He arranged Israel's position so that from every human angle they were finished. Army behind them, see in front of them. No way out. No plan B. And then he told Moses, "I am going to get glory over Pharaoh." He wasn't rescuing them despite the impossible situation. The impossible situation was the plan. Lazarus. John 11. When Jesus heard that Lazarus was sick, scripture says something that most people read too fast. It says, "Now Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus." So when he heard that Lazarus was ill, he stayed 2 days longer in the place where he was. Read that twice. So because he loved them, he waited. The delay was not negligence. It was love with a longer view. He waited until Lazarus was not just dead, but 4 days dead. Past the point where, according to Jewish belief at the time, even the soul had departed. past the point of any possible natural explanation. Past the point where even the people who had watched Jesus heal the blind man were saying, "Could not he who opened the eyes of the blind man also have kept this man from dying past the point where anyone could take credit for what was about to happen?" That is God's pattern. Not intervention before desperation, intervention after desperation has been fully established beyond any shadow of doubt. And here's why it matters for you. If God did this not once, not twice, but every single time across centuries and cultures and completely different situations, then what does that tell you about the impossible situation you are in right now? Let's go through the stories. Case study one, the Red Sea. The morning Israel reached the Red Sea. They had been free for less than a week. 10 plagues, centuries of slavery finally ending. the most powerful nation on earth, releasing 2 million people at once. They left with silver and gold. Scripture says Egypt was plundered. They left in such a rush that their bread didn't have time to rise. They were finally out. And then the Egyptian army appeared on the horizon behind them. Pharaoh had changed his mind. 600 elite chariots, the entire Egyptian military coming at full speed, and in front of them, the Red Sea. What do 2 million people do in that moment? They do what we all do. They panic. They turn on Moses. They say, and this is the actual text, Exodus 14:11, "Was it because there were no graves in Egypt that you brought us to the desert to die? What have you done to us by bringing us out of Egypt? Didn't we say to you in Egypt? Leave us alone. Let us serve the Egyptians. It would have been better for us to serve the Egyptians than to die in the desert. That's not unfaithful people. That's terrified people. People who trusted, left everything, walked out of slavery, and now they're standing between an army and a sea. Their theology had a simple question attached to it. Where is God now? Moses said to them, "Do not be afraid. Stand firm, and you will see the deliverance the Lord will bring you today. The Egyptians you see today, you will never see again. The Lord will fight for you. You need only to be still. And then God said to Moses, "Why are you crying out to me? Tell the Israelites to move on. Move on into the sea." And Moses raised his staff. And the sea parted. But notice what God said before the miracle. Not, "I will open the sea so you can escape." He said, "I will gain glory through Pharaoh and all his army." He said, "The Egyptians will know that I am the Lord." This wasn't a rescue mission. It was a demonstration. And demonstrations require an audience that has already given up. If the sea had parted before the army arrived, Israel would have thanked Moses. They would have called it good fortune, good timing, a strong wind from the east. but with an army behind them and the sea closing the only exit with nowhere to go and nothing left to try. When the water split and a 2 million person nation walked across on dry ground, there was only one explanation. Here is the diagnostic question and I want you to sit with it. Is there a situation in your life right now where you have genuinely run out of options? where you've tried everything you can think of, called everyone you know, and arrived at a dead end that feels like a wall. That might not be the end of the story. That might be where the story actually starts. Case study two, Elijah and the altar. The year was approximately 860 BC. Israel had not seen rain in 3 and 1/2 years. That is not a dry season. That is a national catastrophe. crops dead, livestock gone. Ahab the king had sent messengers across the entire country looking for water. The famine was so severe that scripture records Ahab himself going with Oadiah, the manager of his palace, to personally search for grass to keep his horses and mules alive. Into this wasteland walks Elijah. He calls for a showdown on Mount Carmel. 450 prophets of Baal on one side, one prophet of the God of Israel on the other. Each side builds an altar, prepares a sacrifice, and calls on their god to send fire. The prophets of Baal go first. They call on Baal from morning until noon, nothing. They shout louder, nothing. They dance around the altar, nothing. They slash themselves with swords and spears as was their custom until blood flows. Nothing. Afternoon comes, evening comes. Nothing. Elijah has been watching. And when it's his turn, he does something that defies every human instinct toward winning. He tells the people to fill four large jars with water and pour it on the sacrifice and the wood. pour water on the offering in a drought. They do it. He tells them to do it again. They do. He tells them a third time. By the time they're done, 12 jars of water have been poured over the altar. The wood is soaked. The sacrifice is soaked. The trench he dug around the altar is filled with water. Let that land. He is about to ask God to send fire. He has just made it as difficult as possible for fire to fall. Why? Because Elijah understood something about God's character that most of us miss. God does not need favorable conditions. God does not need your strategy, your resources, or your preparation to be impressive. What God needs, what God wants is a situation where when he moves, no one can look at what happened and call it anything other than God. 12 jars of water on a soaked altar. Wood that cannot burn. A trench full of water, a three-year drought. Elijah prayed 32 words. In Hebrew, 32 words, and the fire fell. It consumed the offering. It consumed the wood. It consumed the stones. It consumed the soil. It licked up every drop of water in the trench. Then the rain came. Here is what I want you to notice about what Elijah did. He did not reduce the impossibility. He increased it. He took an already impossible situation and made it more impossible because he understood that the glory of God is most visible when human explanation is most impossible. He poured water on the altar on purpose. Now, here is the question I want you to sit with. Is there something in your situation right now that you have been trying to make more manageable, more reasonable, more likely to succeed by human standards and God keeps allowing it to become more impossible instead. Maybe he's not failing to help you. Maybe he's pouring water on the altar. Maybe he is increasing the impossibility on purpose so that when he moves, what happens cannot be explained away. Case study three. Gideon's army. Gideon was a farmer hiding in a wine press. That detail matters. He was threshing wheat, hiding underground so the Midianites wouldn't see him and steal his food. He was so terrified of his enemies that he conducted his daily work in secret underground alone. This is the man God sent an angel to with the greeting, "The Lord is with you, mighty warrior." Gideon's first response was essentially, "Have you got the right person?" But eventually, he assembled an army, 32,000 men. Which sounds like a lot until you learn that the Midianite army was so large that scripture compares them to a swarm of locusts. Their camels alone were described as too numerous to count. 32,000 against hundreds of thousands. That is already impossible. And God looked at Gideon's 32,000 men and said, "Too many. Too many against hundreds of thousands. Too many." God told Gideon to announce that anyone who was afraid could go home. 22,000 left. 10,000 remained. And God said, "Still too many. Too many. 10,000. Still too many." Then God created a test. He had Gideon take the men down to the water and watch how they drank. Most knelt down and put their faces to the water. 300 cup the water in their hands and brought it to their mouths. God said, "Those 300 are your army. Send the rest home. 300 men against an army like locusts." Gideon's weapons for the final battle. Torches, trumpets, clay pots, no swords, no shields, no military strategy, torches, trumpets, and clay pots. They surrounded the Midianite camp at night, broke their pots simultaneously, exposed the torches, blew their trumpets, and shouted. The Midianites woke up in chaos, couldn't figure out what was happening, and turned their swords on each other. Israel didn't fight. God did. But here is the reason God did it this way. He said it directly in Judges 7 two. You have too many men. I cannot deliver Midian into their hands. Or Israel would boast against me. My own strength has saved me. He could have given Gideon a bigger army. He could have given them better weapons. He chose not to. He deliberately made the situation more impossible so that when the victory came, no one could point to a general or an army or a strategy and say they did it. The only explanation left standing would be God. The diagnostic question for this one is different. Are you holding on to resources, connections, plans, or abilities that you're trusting more than God? Is it possible that God keeps reducing what you have not to hurt you, but because he's trying to build something that can only be explained by him? 300 men, clay pots, the army of locusts scattered. You can't out strategize what God wants to do without you. Case study four. Lazarus. By the time Jesus arrived in Bethany, Lazarus had been dead 4 days. That number was not incidental. Jewish tradition at the time held that the soul remained near the body for 3 days after death, hoping to return. After 3 days, once decomposition was undeniable, the soul departed. 4 days meant there was no debate, no possible misunderstanding. No, maybe he was just in a deep sleep. 4 days meant Lazarus was gone. Martha met Jesus outside the village. Her first words were, "Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died." That sentence carries years of theology inside it. She believed Jesus could stop death. She did not believe he could reverse it. Her faith was real, but it had a time limit. If he had come before the funeral, maybe. But now, 4 days, the body was already in the tomb. When Mary came to Jesus, she said the same thing. Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died. Both sisters believed in Jesus. Both believed he had power. Both had a theology with a deadline built into it, a point passed which even Jesus could not act. And that deadline had already passed. And scripture says something remarkable. It says Jesus saw Mary weeping and he saw the people who came with her weeping. And John 11:33 says, "He was deeply moved in spirit and troubled. And then Jesus wept. He wept." The son of God, who knew exactly what he was about to do, who had deliberately waited two extra days to make sure Lazarus was 4 days dead, who was 30 seconds away from calling a dead man out of a tomb, wept. Not because he didn't know what would happen, but because death is real. Because grief is real. Because the cost of living in a broken world is real. And he did not bypass the grief to get to the miracle. He wept first. Then he walked to the tomb. Martha said practically, faithfully, honestly, Lord, by this time there is a bad odor, for he has been there 4 days. Jesus said, "Did I not tell you that if you believe, you will see the glory of God?" and he called into a sealed tomb. Lazarus come out and the dead man walked out still wrapped in burial cloths. Still carrying the evidence of 4 days in a grave. Here is what I want you to notice. Martha had a theology with a deadline. She believed in Jesus, genuinely believed, but she had a category called too late that she assumed applied to him, too. She thought the window had closed. She thought the moment for a miracle had passed, and Jesus walked past her deadline to the tomb. Your too late is not his too late. The timeline you have constructed, the window you believe has closed, the situation you have already buried, the hope you have written, the eulogy for Jesus has a different calendar. He doesn't just arrive before things get bad. He waits. He waits until the deadline has passed. He waits until every human explanation is buried in the tomb with Lazarus. And then he calls the diagnostic question. What have you given up on? What have you stopped praying about because it's been too long? It's too far gone. It already had a funeral. That might be the exact thing God is about to call out of a tomb. Case study five. The feeding. Late afternoon somewhere on the far side of the Sea of Galilee. The crowd had followed Jesus since morning, and now there were 5,000 men, plus women and children, far from any town with no food. The disciples came to Jesus with a practical assessment. This is a remote place, and it's already getting late. Send the crowds away so they can go to the villages and buy themselves some food. That is not a failure of faith. That is a reasonable reading of the situation. No food, no nearby source of food, thousands of hungry people. The logical answer was clear. Send them home before dark. Jesus said, "They do not need to go away. You give them her something to eat." The disciples did the math. "We have here only five loaves of bread and two fish. Five loaves, two fish. 5,000 men plus families." Jesus took the five loaves and two fish. He looked up to heaven. He gave thanks. He broke them. He gave them to the disciples to distribute. And somehow in a miracle that no one has ever been able to fully explain, the food multiplied as it was given away. 5,000 men were fed. And then the disciples collected the leftovers. 12 basket fulls, one for each disciple, more leftovers than they started with. But notice the sequence again. The miracle did not happen when there was a little food. It happened when there was absurdly insufficient food. When the disciples had already done the math and concluded it was impossible, we have only five loaves and two fish. That sentence is the setup. That is God's starting point. Not 5,000 loaves and 2,000 fish, which would have been slightly inconvenient, but manageable. Five loaves and two fish and thousands of hungry people. God started with what made no sense and turned it into more than enough. Let me step back and show you what all five of these stories have in common. The Red Sea parted when Israel had nowhere to go. Fire fell on Elijah's altar when it was soaked with 12 jars of water. Gideon defeated an army like locusts with 300 men and clay pots. Lazarus walked out of a tomb 4 days after he was buried. 5,000 people were fed with five loaves and two fish. In every case, the impossibility was total. Human options were exhausted. The situation was past the point where anyone could take credit. And in every case, God moved. Now, here is the one sentence that ties the whole pattern together. And I want you to hear it carefully. God does not start with plenty because plenty would make his provision look like your management. He starts with nothing because nothing leaves only one explanation. This is not a pattern about God being dramatic. It is a pattern about God being unmistakable. When the impossible becomes possible, there is no debate about where it came from. You cannot attribute it to good strategy. You cannot call it favorable circumstances. You cannot point to your skills or your network or your plan. When dead men walk and waters split and fires fall on soaked altars, only one name fits in the blank. Now, I need to give you the warning because this pattern can be misread. This is not a promise that every dead situation in your life will have a Lazarus moment. Not every story in the Bible ends in miraculous rescue. John the Baptist's story ended in prison. Steven's story ended with stones. Paul's thorn was never removed. God's definition of miracle may not look like yours. Sometimes the miracle is peace in the impossible situation, not escape from it. Sometimes the miracle is who you become in the waiting, not the removal of the weight. Sometimes the glory of God is revealed not by making the impossible possible but by sustaining his people through the impossible with a steadiness that cannot be explained any other way. So I am not telling you that your red sea will split or your dead situation will walk out of a tomb. I am telling you something more important than that. I am telling you that God has never once in all of scripture been limited by the impossibility of a situation. He has never arrived at a dead end and said, "I can't work here." Every single time human ability ran out, his began. The situation you are in right now, however impossible, however past deadline, however many jars of water seem to have already been poured, is not beyond him. The morning the Red Sea parted, the Israelites went to sleep trapped. They had no reason to believe the next day would be different from the one they just survived. The army was still behind them. The sea was still in front of them. Nothing had changed overnight. And then Moses raised his staff and everything changed. They could not have planned for it. They could not have engineered it. They had no part in making it happen. The only thing they did that morning was wake up and face the situation they were still in. And God moved. I don't know what your Red Sea looks like. I don't know what has been in front of you that feels impossible. What has been behind you that feels like it's closing in? What you've been staring at so long, you've stopped believing it could ever change. But I know this. The pattern in this book is not about people who had it figured out.
